meta.blurb: We are not the strongest animal, or the fastest, or the oldest. So how did one species from Africa end up filling every continent, building cities and walking on the Moon? Follow the whole story, from the first stone tool to the world of eight billion.
meta.bible: Homo sapiens: our own species, which appeared in Africa at least 300,000 years ago; every person alive today belongs to it. Neanderthals: a human species of Europe and Western Asia, died out about 40,000 years ago. Denisovans: another human species, known mostly from bones and teeth found in Siberia and Tibet. Homo erectus, Homo floresiensis: other human species. Places: Africa, Morocco, Europe, Asia, Israel, Australia, Indonesia, Flores, Siberia, Alaska, Americas, Fertile Crescent, Middle East, China, Mexico, New Guinea, Turkey, Mesopotamia, Uruk, Babylon, Egypt, Nile, Giza, Indus, Persia, Lydia, Rome, Baghdad, Germany, Britain, Atlantic, Jupiter, Moon, Mississippi. People: Hammurabi: king of Babylon about 3,700 years ago. Khufu: the pharaoh who built the Great Pyramid. Confucius, the Buddha, Socrates: thinkers of about 2,500 years ago. Johannes Gutenberg: printer of Germany, about 1450. Christopher Columbus: sailed in 1492. Galileo: used a telescope in 1610. Isaac Newton: published his laws in 1687. Edward Jenner: used a safe injection against smallpox in 1796. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch: German chemists who found how to make fertiliser from air. Wilbur and Orville Wright: flew in 1903. Yuri Gagarin: first person in space, 1961. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin: first on the Moon, 1969. Key terms: Çatalhöyük, Ancestor, Species, Fossil, Hunter, Gatherer, Forager, Ice Age, Megafauna, Mammoth, Sloth, Fertile, Domesticated, Surplus, Scribe, Cuneiform, Tablet, Bronze, Iron, Bartering, Currency, Empire, Silk Road, Plague, Printing press, Telegraph, Steam, Factories, Vaccine, Smallpox, Fertiliser, Nitrogen, Carbon dioxide, Biomass, DNA, Internet. Dates are given as about where they are uncertain; Homo sapiens fossils from Morocco are about 300,000 years old; the first writing, in Uruk, about 5,300 years ago; the first coins, in Lydia, about 2,600 years ago; the Black Death, 1347 to 1351; the world's population passed one billion about 1800 and eight billion in 2022. Voice and tone: wondering, clear and fair; each beat explains one step in the human story in plain words; scientists' disagreements are stated honestly; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; hard parts of history (slavery, disease, war, harm to nature) are told factually and without gore.

beats.scene: A small group of people look out over a wide plain at sunrise
beats.summary: Humans are one species among millions, yet we have changed the whole planet; this book follows the journey from a small group in Africa to a world of eight billion.

beats.scene: A few early people walk across a grassy African plain at dawn
beats.summary: Our species, Homo sapiens, first appeared in Africa at least 300,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A Neanderthal family sits beside a fire in a cold, snowy landscape
beats.summary: Homo sapiens was never alone: Neanderthals, Denisovans and other human species lived at the same time.

beats.scene: An early human ancestor walks upright through tall grass carrying a stick
beats.summary: Millions of years earlier, our ancestors began to walk on two legs, which freed their hands.

beats.scene: Hands strike one stone against another to make a sharp flake
beats.summary: Early humans learned to make sharp stone tools, which could cut meat and crack bones.

beats.scene: People sit in a circle around a crackling fire in a dark cave
beats.summary: At some point our ancestors learned to control fire, giving warmth, light and protection; scientists disagree about when.

beats.scene: A person turns a piece of meat over hot stones beside a fire
beats.summary: Cooking made food softer and easier to digest, and may have helped to feed the energy-hungry human brain.

beats.scene: A small band of people walk in a line across dry grassland
beats.summary: For almost all of history, people lived in small bands, hunting and gathering and sharing what they found.

beats.scene: Two people talk and point toward the horizon beside a campfire
beats.summary: Nobody knows when language began, but speech let people warn, teach, plan and describe things that were not in front of them.

beats.scene: Painted animals and red handprints glow on a cave wall in torchlight
beats.summary: At least 40,000 years ago people were painting animals on cave walls and making beads, which show imagination and shared ideas.

beats.scene: Travellers walk in a line along a coast beside a wide blue sea
beats.summary: Some groups left Africa long ago, but the main spread of our species across the world seems to have begun about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A modern and an ancient face side by side, with a thread linking them
beats.summary: Our ancestors sometimes had children with Neanderthals and Denisovans, so a little of their DNA lives on in many people today.

beats.scene: A last Neanderthal stands alone at the entrance of a cave at dusk
beats.summary: The Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago, and the other human species also vanished; scientists do not agree on why.

beats.scene: People on a simple raft paddle across open sea towards a distant shore
beats.summary: People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, which required crossing open sea in boats or rafts.

beats.scene: Hunters in furs walk across a snowy land between two vast icy seas
beats.summary: During the last Ice Age, lower seas opened a route between Siberia and Alaska, and people reached the Americas at least 15,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A huge woolly mammoth stands in snow while small hunters watch from far away
beats.summary: As people spread, many giant animals died out, and scientists think hunting and a changing climate both played a part.

beats.scene: Green plants and wild grasses cover a warm valley beside a river
beats.summary: About 11,700 years ago the last Ice Age ended, and the warmer, steadier climate gave people new chances to find and grow food.

beats.scene: Women harvest wild grain with stone blades beside round stone houses
beats.summary: In some places, such as the Middle East, wild food was so rich that people settled in villages about 14,000 years ago, long before farming.

beats.scene: Farmers scatter seed and cut ripe wheat in a sunny field
beats.summary: About 11,000 years ago people in the Fertile Crescent began to plant crops; farming began independently in several other places too.

beats.scene: A farmer leads a sheep and a goat past a small mud house
beats.summary: People tamed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, and learned to use them for meat, milk and wool; dogs had joined people earlier.

beats.scene: A tired farmer bends over a field while a hunter rests nearby
beats.summary: Farming fed more people per field, but early farmers often worked harder, ate less varied food and caught diseases from animals.

beats.scene: Flat-roofed mud houses packed together with people climbing ladders on the roofs
beats.summary: Some villages grew into towns; Çatalhöyük in Turkey, about 9,000 years ago, had houses so close together that people walked on the roofs.

beats.scene: Workers pour grain into a large storehouse while a ruler watches
beats.summary: Stored grain was a kind of wealth; those who controlled it often became rulers, and inequality grew.

beats.scene: A scribe presses marks into a soft clay tablet with a reed
beats.summary: Writing began about 5,300 years ago in Mesopotamia, first for keeping accounts of grain, beer and cloth.

beats.scene: A tall stone with carved writing stands in a crowded city square
beats.summary: Large cities needed shared rules; about 3,700 years ago King Hammurabi of Babylon had nearly 300 laws carved on a stone for all to see.

beats.scene: A great stone pyramid rises beside a river with workers and boats
beats.summary: In Egypt, beside the Nile, the Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago as a royal tomb, showing how many people a ruler could organise.

beats.scene: A wooden cart, a horse and a sailing boat beside a river
beats.summary: The wheel, tamed horses and sailing ships made it faster and cheaper to carry goods and people over long distances.

beats.scene: A smith pours glowing bronze into a mould beside a hot furnace
beats.summary: People learned to mix copper and tin to make bronze about 5,000 years ago, and later used iron, which was cheaper and strong.

beats.scene: A merchant weighs silver on a scale while a customer holds out a coin
beats.summary: Trade became easier with money; the first coins we know of were made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, about 2,600 years ago.

beats.scene: A long road with riders and messengers crossing a wide sandy landscape
beats.summary: Large empires such as Persia, Rome and Qin China used roads, messengers and armies to rule huge areas.

beats.scene: A caravan of camels carries bundles of silk along a desert road
beats.summary: From about 2,100 years ago, roads and sea routes linked China with the Mediterranean, carrying silk, spices, ideas and diseases.

beats.scene: Three thinkers in different robes sit under trees, speaking to students
beats.summary: Around 2,500 years ago, thinkers such as Confucius, the Buddha and Socrates asked how people should live, and many beliefs spread widely afterwards.

beats.scene: Scholars read and copy books in a bright library with tall shelves
beats.summary: In places such as Baghdad, about 1,200 years ago, scholars translated and added to the world's knowledge; numbers from India, including zero, reached Europe through them.

beats.scene: A quiet empty street in a medieval town with closed doors
beats.summary: The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 spread along trade routes and may have killed a third or more of the people in Europe.

beats.scene: A printer pulls the lever of a wooden press beside a pile of pages
beats.summary: Around 1450, Gutenberg's press with movable metal type made books cheaper and ideas faster to spread.

beats.scene: A wooden sailing ship with three masts crosses wide waves under a bright sun
beats.summary: In 1492 Columbus crossed the Atlantic and reached the Americas, beginning lasting contact between the hemispheres; ships soon sailed around the world.

beats.scene: Crops, animals and ships crossing between two continents on a map
beats.summary: After 1492, crops, animals and diseases crossed the ocean in both directions; diseases killed huge numbers of people in the Americas.

beats.scene: A large ship at a harbour with people in chains waiting on the quay
beats.summary: From the 1500s to the 1800s, more than 10 million people were taken from Africa and forced to work as slaves in the Americas.

beats.scene: A man looks through a long brass telescope at the night sky
beats.summary: From the 1500s a new way of finding out spread, based on observation and experiment; Galileo's telescope in 1610 showed moons around Jupiter.

beats.scene: A steam engine drives machines in a large smoky factory hall
beats.summary: From about 1760, Britain began to use coal, steam engines and factories on a large scale, and many people moved to cities.

beats.scene: A steam train crosses a hill while a man taps a telegraph key
beats.summary: In the 1800s railways and the telegraph made travel and news much faster.

beats.scene: A graph line curving steeply upwards beside crowds of people
beats.summary: The human population passed one billion about 1800, and reached eight billion in 2022.

beats.scene: A doctor gives an injection to a child while a nurse looks on
beats.summary: Vaccines, clean water and better medicine let people live much longer; smallpox was wiped out by 1980.

beats.scene: A farmer spreads fertiliser on a green field of tall wheat
beats.summary: In the early 1900s two German chemists, Haber and Bosch, found how to make fertiliser from the air; many experts think about half of us now eat food grown with it.

beats.scene: A destroyed street at dusk with a lone figure and a distant glow
beats.summary: The two world wars of 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945 killed tens of millions of people, and the first atomic bombs showed the power of modern weapons.

beats.scene: A small propeller aeroplane in the air and a rocket on a launch pad
beats.summary: In 1903 the Wright brothers made the first powered flight; 66 years later, in 1969, humans walked on the Moon.

beats.scene: A person holds a glowing phone beside a very old room-sized computer
beats.summary: Computers, once as big as rooms, became tiny and powerful; the web began about 1990, and more than five billion people now use the internet.

beats.scene: Smoking chimneys and a busy road under a hazy evening sky
beats.summary: Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air, and the planet has warmed by a little more than one degree Celsius.

beats.scene: A wild animal watches from a forest edge beside fields of cattle
beats.summary: Humans and their farm animals now make up most of the weight of all mammals, and many wild species are in danger as their homes shrink.

beats.scene: People of many ages and skin colours stand together looking at the sunrise
beats.summary: All people alive today are one species with almost identical DNA; the story is unfinished, and the choices we make now will shape the next chapter.

B1B2: Humans are only one of millions of kinds of animal on Earth. Yet no other animal has built cities, crossed oceans or left footprints on the Moon.
The oldest bones that look like ours were found in Africa. They are about 300,000 years old, although scientists still argue about exactly where and when our species began.
Our species was never alone on Earth. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, and other groups, such as the Denisovans, lived farther east.
Millions of years before our species appeared, our ancestors began to walk upright. This freed their hands, so they could carry food, look after babies and, later, make tools.
Some of the oldest stone tools ever found are about three million years old. By striking one stone against another, early toolmakers made sharp edges that could cut meat.
At some point, our ancestors learned to control fire. Scientists disagree about exactly when, with some evidence going back about a million years, but fire clearly changed life.
Cooking makes food softer and much easier for the body to digest. Many scientists think that it gave our ancestors extra energy to feed their large brains, although the details are still debated.
For most of human history, people lived in small groups of a few dozen. They moved from place to place, hunting animals and gathering plants, and they shared what they found.
Nobody knows exactly when human language began, because words leave no bones behind. But once people could describe the past and plan the future, they could cooperate much better.
At least 40,000 years ago, people were painting animals on cave walls and making jewellery from beads and shells. These things suggest that they could imagine, and that they had ideas to share.
Small groups of our species left Africa more than once. But the main wave that spread across the world probably began about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago.
When our ancestors met Neanderthals, some of them had children together. As a result, many people today carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA, usually one or two per cent.

The Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago, and the other human species disappeared too. Scientists are not sure why, but climate change, small numbers and competition probably all played a part.
People first reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago. There was always sea between Australia and Asia, so the first travellers must have crossed the water on boats or rafts.
During the last Ice Age, so much water was frozen that the sea level dropped. People then moved from Asia into the Americas, and they arrived at least 15,000 years ago, and perhaps earlier.
Around the same time, many giant animals vanished, including mammoths and giant sloths. Scientists still argue about the cause, but hunting and a changing climate both probably played a part.
About 11,700 years ago, the last Ice Age ended, and the climate became warmer and steadier. This gave people new chances to find and grow food.
In some places, wild food was so plentiful that people stopped moving around. About 14,000 years ago, people in the Middle East were already living in villages and gathering wild grains.
Around 11,000 years ago, people in the Middle East began to plant wheat and barley. Farming also began on its own in China, Mexico, New Guinea and other places.
At about the same time, people began to keep animals. Sheep, goats, cattle and pigs were slowly tamed, and dogs had probably been living with people for even longer.
A farm can feed far more people than hunting can on the same land. But early farmers often worked harder, ate a less varied diet and caught diseases from their animals.
Farm villages grew bigger and bigger over time. About 9,000 years ago, in a town called Çatalhöyük in Turkey, the houses were packed so closely together that people walked across the roofs.
Grain can be stored for many months, so farmers could save food for later. Whoever controlled the stores gained power, and in many places this made society more unequal.
Writing began in Mesopotamia about 5,300 years ago, and it was first used for counting, not for telling stories. Clay tablets recorded how much grain, beer and cloth people owned or owed.
As cities grew, rulers needed rules for the strangers who lived in them. About 3,700 years ago, King Hammurabi of Babylon had a long list of laws carved on a tall stone.

Early civilisations grew beside great rivers, such as the Nile in Egypt. The Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago as a tomb for a king, and it was the tallest building in the world for centuries.
About 5,500 years ago, people began to use wheels for carts. Later, horses were tamed and sailing ships carried goods along rivers and coasts, so trade grew.

About 5,000 years ago, people learned to mix copper with tin to make bronze, a metal that is harder than copper. Around 3,200 years ago, iron began to be widely used, because it was cheaper and strong.
Trade became easier when people agreed to use pieces of metal as money. The first coins that we know about were made in the kingdom of Lydia, in modern Turkey, about 2,600 years ago.
Around 2,500 years ago, the Persian Empire stretched across a huge area of Asia, Africa and Europe. It used roads and relay messengers to keep control of such a large area.
From about 2,100 years ago, a network of roads and sea routes linked China with the lands around the Mediterranean. Silk, spices, paper and new ideas travelled along them, and so did diseases.

About 2,500 years ago, thinkers such as Confucius in China, the Buddha in India and Socrates in Greece asked how people ought to live. Their questions and teachings are still discussed by many people today.

In cities such as Baghdad, about 1,200 years ago, scholars translated books from many languages and added their own discoveries. Numbers from India, including the zero, reached Europe through the Arab world.
Between 1347 and 1351, a terrible disease called the Black Death spread across Europe, Asia and North Africa along the trade routes. It may have killed a third of the people in Europe.
Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg in Germany built a printing press that used movable metal letters. Books became cheaper to make, so more people learned to read, and ideas spread faster.
In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed across the Atlantic and reached islands in the Americas. His voyage began lasting contact between the Americas and the rest of the world.

After 1492, crops such as potatoes, maize and tomatoes travelled from the Americas to the rest of the world. Horses, cattle and wheat crossed the ocean the other way, and so did diseases, which killed huge numbers of people.
From the 1500s to the 1800s, more than 10 million people were taken from Africa across the Atlantic and forced to work as slaves. It was one of the greatest crimes in human history.
From the 1500s, a new way of finding things out spread, based on careful observation and experiment. In 1610, Galileo used a telescope to see moons moving around Jupiter.
From about 1760, Britain began to use coal, steam engines and factories on a large scale. Goods that once took weeks to make by hand could be made much faster, and many people moved to the cities.
In the 1800s, railways carried people and goods faster than any horse could. The telegraph sent messages along wires, so news could cross a country in minutes instead of weeks.
For most of history, fewer than a billion people lived on Earth. We passed one billion about the year 1800, and by 2022, there were eight billion of us.
In 1796, Edward Jenner showed that an injection could protect people from smallpox, a deadly disease. In 1980, the World Health Organization announced that smallpox had been wiped out completely.

In the early 1900s, two German chemists, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch, found a way to make fertiliser from the nitrogen in the air. Many experts think that about half of the people alive today eat food grown with it.

The First World War, from 1914 to 1918, and the Second World War, from 1939 to 1945, caused terrible suffering. Tens of millions of people died, and in 1945 the first atomic bombs showed how powerful our weapons had become.
In 1903, the Wright brothers made the first powered flight in an aeroplane. Only 66 years later, in 1969, astronauts walked on the Moon.
The first electronic computers filled whole rooms in the 1940s. Today, a phone that fits in a pocket is far more powerful, and more than five billion people use the internet.

When we burn coal, oil and gas, we release carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the air. The amount in the air has risen from about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution to more than 420 today.
Scientists estimate that people and their farm animals now make up most of the weight of all the mammals on Earth. Many wild species are in danger because we are taking over their homes.
All people alive today belong to one species, and our genes are almost the same. The story is not finished, and the choices we make will shape the next chapter.
C1C2: Among the millions of species that share this planet, we are neither the strongest, nor the fastest, nor the oldest. And yet, in a very short span of time, we have built cities, filled the sky with aircraft and left our footprints on the Moon. This book follows that long and surprising journey, from a small group of people in Africa to a world of eight billion.

The oldest known bones that look like ours were found in Morocco, and they are about 300,000 years old, which shows how ancient our species really is. Scientists still argue about where in Africa we first appeared, because early people may have lived in several places that were linked by travel and marriage. What is clear is that every person alive today descends from people who once lived on that continent.

For most of our history we shared the planet with other kinds of human beings. The Neanderthals, who were strong and stocky, lived in the cold lands of Europe and western Asia, while the Denisovans, known mostly from a few bones and teeth, lived farther to the east. A small kind of human, nicknamed the hobbit, even lived on the island of Flores in Indonesia until perhaps 50,000 years ago.

The story really begins millions of years before Homo sapiens, when some apes in Africa started to spend more of their time walking upright on two legs. Scientists argue about the reasons, which may have included seeing over tall grass or carrying food and children, but the result was that the hands were free for new tasks. Those hands would one day shape stones, paint pictures on cave walls and finally write down the words of the world's many languages.

The oldest stone tools yet found are about three million years old, and many were made by species that came long before ours. By striking one stone against another, early toolmakers produced sharp flakes that could cut meat, scrape skins and crack open bones to reach the rich marrow inside. A tool, in other words, was a way of borrowing the teeth and claws that these creatures did not have.

At some point, our ancestors learned to keep a fire burning, and this may have been among the most important steps in the whole story. Scientists still disagree about when it first happened, with some evidence reaching back about a million years and firmer proof from much later. Fire gave warmth in the cold, light after dark, protection from hungry animals and, above all, a way to change food.

Cooking breaks down tough fibres and makes many foods easier to digest, so that more of their energy reaches the body. The human brain is about three times the size of a chimpanzee's and uses roughly a fifth of our energy even at rest. Many scientists believe that cooked food helped to pay that bill, although the idea is still debated. Whatever the full truth, a meal shared by the fire gave people a reason to sit together and talk.

For almost all of our history, people lived in small bands of perhaps a few dozen, moving with the seasons to hunt animals and gather fruit, roots and nuts. Everyone knew everyone else, and survival depended on sharing food, caring for children together and passing on what each person had learned. It was a life of close cooperation, though on a very small scale, and the great change in later chapters was to make it larger.

No one knows when people first began to speak in full sentences, because words leave no fossils, and scientists have suggested dates that stretch across hundreds of thousands of years. What is certain is that language changed our lives, for it allowed us to warn of danger, to teach skills, to plan a hunt and to describe things that were not in front of us. A single clever person could now pass a good idea to a whole group in an afternoon.

On cave walls in Europe and in Indonesia, people left paintings of animals and handprints that are at least 40,000 years old, and in Africa they were making beads from shells even earlier. These objects had no use for survival, which is exactly why they matter, since they reveal minds that could imagine and symbolise. A painted bison on a wall is a message across time, and we are still reading it.

There were several early journeys out of Africa, and fossils found in Israel suggest that some of our kind had reached the Middle East more than 170,000 years ago. Most people living outside Africa today, however, descend from a larger movement that is thought to have begun some 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. They travelled slowly, one generation at a time, following rivers, coastlines and herds of animals, with no idea that they were crossing continents.

When Homo sapiens met the Neanderthals in Europe and Asia, the two groups sometimes had children together, and we know this because the evidence is written in our DNA. People whose families come from outside Africa usually carry one or two per cent Neanderthal DNA, and some people in Asia and the Pacific carry a small share from the Denisovans as well. In a very real sense, those other humans did not vanish entirely, because a little of them lives on in us.

The last Neanderthals disappeared about 40,000 years ago, and the other human species vanished too, leaving Homo sapiens as the only kind of human on Earth. Scientists do not agree on the reasons, and most suspect a mixture of changing climate, small and scattered populations, competition for food and, perhaps, mixing with our own larger groups. It is a reminder that survival was never guaranteed, even for the cleverest of creatures.

Australia was reached by people at least 50,000 years ago, and some evidence suggests that the first arrivals came even earlier. Because there was always open water between that continent and Asia, even when the sea was low, those early travellers must have built boats or rafts of some kind, and they sailed without a map or a compass. Their descendants have lived there ever since, and their cultures are among the oldest that still continue today.

During the last Ice Age so much of the world's water was locked up in ice that the sea fell, and a stretch of land appeared between Siberia and Alaska. Groups of people moved into the Americas by land, by boat along the coast, or perhaps by both, and they had arrived at least 15,000 years ago, although some discoveries hint at an earlier date. Within a few thousand years their descendants had spread to the southern tip of South America, which was a journey of many thousands of miles.

As people spread into new lands, many of the largest animals disappeared, including woolly mammoths, giant ground sloths and huge kangaroo-like creatures. Scientists still argue about the causes, and most believe that a warming climate and hunting by humans combined, with the balance differing from place to place. Whatever the exact mixture, it was one of the first signs that our species could change an entire living world.

About 11,700 years ago the last Ice Age came to an end, and the world entered a warmer and steadier period that has lasted until today. Forests spread, rivers filled and wild grasses covered wide areas where there had once been cold, dry plains. For the people who lived there, it was the start of a new chapter in which the climate was kind enough to allow experiments.

In some regions the wild food was so rich that groups no longer needed to move, and by about 14,000 years ago people in the Middle East were living in permanent villages of stone houses. They gathered wild wheat and barley, ground them into flour and stored them, long before anyone had planted a single seed. Staying in one place changed a great deal, because it encouraged people to own things, to build things and to have more children.

Around 11,000 years ago, people in the region known as the Fertile Crescent began to plant and harvest wheat, barley and lentils, rather than only gathering them from the wild. The same thing happened independently in several other places, including China, where people grew rice and millet, and Mexico, where they grew maize and squash. Farming was not a single invention, but a discovery made again and again as the climate allowed.

Alongside the plants came the animals, as people gradually tamed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, and learned to use them for meat, milk, wool and, later, for pulling ploughs. The dog had joined humans much earlier, perhaps more than 15,000 years ago, although the exact date is debated. A farm was a new kind of partnership, and it made human beings depend on creatures that, in turn, depended on them.

A field of grain can feed many more people than the same land used for hunting, and so populations grew quickly in farming regions. The bones of early farmers, however, often show signs of harder work, poorer diets and new diseases that passed to people from their animals. It was a trade, in other words, and scholars still debate whether it made ordinary lives better or worse at the start.

Some farming villages grew into towns, and one of the best known is Çatalhöyük in what is now Turkey, which was lived in from about 9,000 years ago. Its mud-brick houses were packed so tightly together that there were no streets, and people came and went across the roofs and climbed down ladders into their homes. Several thousand people may have lived there at its largest, though experts disagree about the exact number.

Grain can be stored for months or even years, and that simple fact had large consequences, because whoever controlled the stores controlled a kind of wealth. In many places, people who guarded the harvest, led the ceremonies or commanded the fighters became rulers, and their families grew richer than their neighbours. Inequality was not new, but stored wealth made it far easier to pass on from parent to child.

The oldest known writing appeared in the city of Uruk, in Mesopotamia, about 5,300 years ago, and it was not poetry or history but accounts. Scribes pressed marks into soft clay to record how much grain, beer and cloth had been received or owed, and the marks later grew into a script that could capture speech. Writing gave people a memory outside the human brain, so a promise could now outlast the person who made it.

Strangers who lived side by side in large cities needed rules, and rulers began to write them down. About 3,700 years ago, King Hammurabi of Babylon had nearly 300 laws carved onto a tall stone, so that anyone who could read, or find someone who could, would know what was expected. The laws were often harsh by modern standards, and punishments depended on a person's rank, yet the idea that rules should be public was an important step.

The first great civilisations grew up beside rivers, which provided water, rich soil and an easy way to travel, and in Egypt the Nile gave life to a kingdom that lasted for thousands of years. About 4,500 years ago the pharaoh Khufu had the Great Pyramid of Giza built as his tomb, and it remained the tallest building in the world for nearly 4,000 years. It stands as proof of how many people one ruler could feed, organise and direct.

The wheel appears to have been invented about 5,500 years ago, and before long it was carrying loads, pulling carts and, eventually, rolling into battle in chariots. Horses were tamed some time later, and sailing ships carried cargo along rivers and coasts, so that goods which had once travelled only a few miles could now cross seas. Each of these advances made the world a little smaller, and made trading far more profitable.

Early metalworkers discovered that mixing copper with a little tin produced bronze, a metal that is harder than either, and by about 5,000 years ago it was being used for tools, ornaments and weapons. Around 3,200 years ago iron began to be used more widely, because its ore was far more common than copper or tin, and so strong tools and blades became cheaper. Whole periods of history are named after these metals, which shows how much they mattered.

Trading by swapping goods works badly, because the person who has what you want may not want what you have. Lumps of silver and other metals solved part of this problem, and about 2,600 years ago the kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey, began to stamp small pieces of metal so that their weight and value could be trusted. Money is useful only because people believe in it, and that shared trust made trading with strangers much easier.

Around 2,500 years ago the Persian Empire ruled a vast area from Egypt to northern India, and it kept control with well-built roads, local governors and relay riders who carried messages across great distances. Later, in China, the Qin dynasty united many states in 221 BCE, and Rome came to dominate the whole Mediterranean. Each empire collected taxes, built roads and spread its language, and in doing so, each one connected many different peoples.

From about 2,100 years ago, a network of roads and sea routes known today as the Silk Roads connected China with India, the Middle East and the Mediterranean. Merchants carried silk, spices, glass and paper across thousands of miles, and travelling alongside them were religions, inventions, stories and diseases. No single trader made the whole journey, but the goods passed from hand to hand, linking people who never knew of each other.

In the same few centuries, around 2,500 years ago, thinkers in different parts of the world began to ask how people ought to live. Confucius in China, the Buddha in India and Socrates in Greece never met, yet each taught that people should think carefully about their actions, and their followers wrote their words down. Over the following centuries, many religions and philosophies spread across continents, bringing millions of strangers into communities of shared belief.

In cities such as Baghdad, about 1,200 years ago, scholars gathered books from Greece, India, Persia and elsewhere, translated them into Arabic and added discoveries of their own in mathematics, medicine and astronomy. The system of numbers that we use today, with its useful zero, came from India and reached Europe largely through Arabic books. Knowledge, it turns out, grows best when it is allowed to travel and to be shared.

Between 1347 and 1351 a terrible disease, which we now call the Black Death, travelled along trade routes and swept through Europe, Asia and North Africa. Estimates of the deaths vary widely, but historians think that perhaps a third or more of Europe's people died, and whole villages were left empty. The disaster showed how a connected world could spread germs as quickly as goods, a lesson that would be learned again and again.

Around 1450, a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press that used movable metal letters, an idea that printers in East Asia had already tried in other forms. Within a few decades presses were running in dozens of cities, and books that had once taken months to copy by hand could be produced in large numbers. Reading spread, arguments spread, and new ideas could now cross a continent faster than any army.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus sailed west across the Atlantic and reached islands in the Caribbean, which began a lasting connection between the Americas and the rest of the world, although Viking sailors had touched North America some 500 years earlier. Millions of people already lived in the Americas, and they had their own cities, farms and traditions. Within thirty years a Spanish expedition had sailed all the way around the globe, and the world's oceans had become a single, connected network.

After 1492, crops from the Americas, including potatoes, maize and tomatoes, spread across the world and changed what people ate, while horses, cattle and wheat travelled in the other direction. Diseases such as smallpox and measles went with them, and because people in the Americas had no earlier experience of these illnesses, many communities suffered terribly. Estimates of the numbers who died vary widely, but historians agree that it was one of the greatest disasters in human history.

From the 1500s until the 1800s, more than 10 million people were seized in Africa, shipped across the Atlantic in terrible conditions and forced to work as slaves on plantations and in mines. Many died on the journey, and those who survived were separated from their families and treated as property. The wealth that the trade created helped to build great cities and fortunes, and its effects on people's lives and on societies can still be felt today.

Scholars in many lands had studied nature for centuries, but from the 1500s a new habit spread through Europe: test your ideas against careful observations, and be ready to change them. In 1610 Galileo turned a telescope towards Jupiter and saw small moons circling it, and in 1687 Isaac Newton published laws that explained the motion of falling apples and orbiting planets alike. Knowledge grew because people learned to say that they did not know, and then to find out.

From about 1760, first in Britain and then elsewhere, coal-fired steam engines began to drive machines in large factories, and goods that had once been made slowly by hand could now be produced in great quantities. Millions of people moved from villages to fast-growing cities to find work, where conditions were often crowded, dirty and dangerous. The Industrial Revolution made many people richer in the long run, but it changed ordinary life faster than any earlier change.

In the 1800s, railways carried people and goods across countries at a speed that no horse could match, and journeys that had once taken weeks could be made in a day. Meanwhile the telegraph, which sent signals along wires, turned news into something that could cross a continent, and later the ocean, in minutes. Time itself became more standard, since a train needed a timetable that made sense in every town.

For most of history the human population grew very slowly, and fewer than a billion people lived on Earth until about the year 1800. After that it began to climb at an astonishing rate, passing two billion in the 1920s and reaching eight billion in 2022, according to the United Nations. Never before had one large animal become so numerous, and feeding and housing so many people has been one of the great challenges of modern times.

In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner showed that a safe injection could protect people against smallpox, and later discoveries about germs, clean water and medicines saved countless lives. In 1980 the World Health Organization announced that smallpox, which had killed millions of people through the centuries, had been wiped out completely. Across the world, average life expectancy has roughly doubled since 1800, which counts among the greatest gains in human history.

Plants need nitrogen to grow, and although the air is full of it, plants cannot use it in that form, so farmers had long depended on manure and a few natural supplies. In the early 1900s the German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch worked out how to turn nitrogen from the air into fertiliser on a large scale. Many experts believe that about half of the world's people are now fed with food grown with its help. It is a good example of how a single idea can quietly feed billions.

The First World War, from 1914 to 1918, and the Second World War, from 1939 to 1945, were fought with machines that could kill on a scale never seen before, and tens of millions of people died. In 1945 the first atomic bombs were used, and for the first time in history a single weapon could destroy a whole city. Out of this horror came the United Nations, which was founded that same year in the hope that countries might settle their quarrels without war.

In 1903 two brothers named Wilbur and Orville Wright flew a flimsy aeroplane for twelve seconds above a beach in North Carolina, and it was the first powered flight with a person on board. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person to travel in space, and in 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Moon, just 66 years after the Wrights' first flight. No earlier generation had seen change on such a scale within a single lifetime.

The first electronic computers of the 1940s filled whole rooms, cost a fortune and could do only a tiny fraction of what a modern phone can do. The World Wide Web appeared around 1990, and since then the internet has linked more than five billion people, so that a question asked in one country can be answered within seconds by someone in another. We have never before been able to share so much information so quickly, and we are still learning how to use it wisely.

When we burn coal, oil and gas, we release carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere, and the amount in the air has risen from about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution to more than 420 today. Scientists are in strong agreement that this is the main reason why the Earth has warmed by a little more than one degree Celsius since the late 1800s. How warm it becomes in future depends on the choices that people make in this century, which gives us both a serious problem and a real chance to act.

Scientists who have tried to weigh all the mammals on Earth estimate that humans and our farm animals now make up the great majority of the total, while wild mammals account for only a small fraction. Many wild species are in danger because farms, cities and roads have taken over the places where they once lived, and some have already vanished for ever. Yet there are also success stories, in which people have protected habitats and saved species such as whales and eagles from disappearing.

All people alive today belong to a single species, and our DNA is almost exactly the same, whatever country we come from or language we speak. We took over the world not because we were the strongest, but because we learned to share what we know, from the first spoken word to the latest discovery. What happens in the next chapter will depend on whether we can use that knowledge with care, for each other and for the planet that we all share.
